title: Compressing horizontal distance but not height: a shader warp that makes distant landmarks loom above.
author: yaosio
selftext:
Try it here. This is just a tech demo. https://claude.ai/artifact/327mwcbU2kuKtvVVnSnXPe

While trying to create an effect I saw in an AI generate a video Claude Opus 5.5 came across this really neat effect. This is a real-time vertex warp. Past a set distance from the player, the world is pulled in horizontally but keeps its full height.

What it does depends on where you look. Anything above eye level, like a tower or a mountain, gets drawn closer but just as tall, so it looms over you and holds that height as you walk toward it. Anything below eye level does the opposite: from up high, the ground drops away steeply, so the world below looks much farther away than it really is.

It's one formula in the vertex shader, based only on where the player stands, so turning doesn't change anything. Objects crossing the boundary bend smoothly back into normal 3D.

Additionally a pixelated effect has been added along with dithering making it reminiscent of a 90s adventure game with really low res pictures. There is also a day night cycle.

comments.author: mattisverywhack
comments.body: Holy shit! Nice work. I feel like games have been trying to figure this out forever and you’ve done it

replies.author: yaosio
replies.body:
Claude figured it out, not me. To be fair it got the final idea from my description of how I thought it would work. It didn't do it the way I said but did use a boundry. I would never have been able to do any of this without Claude, I know nothing about to rogramming or graphics.

I said Imagine a boundry where anything past or is flattened to 2D and placed on the boundry. As this boundary moves through the world the 3D world extrudes through the boundary. So if you were looking side on you would see it appearing out of nothing. On the boundary the 2D object is enlarged and warped so it's edges  meets the 3D self correctly. You never see the transition between 2D and 3D because everything meets at the boundary. There's no weirdness as you turn because the warp effect always meets at the boundry.

All the other ideas it and me came up with had various issues where it didn't work as intended.

comments.author: Ravesoull
comments.body:
It’s good, but still not quite the right effect. It feels like something trying to approximate it, and I respect your effort in trying to recreate it, but in your case, it comes out as some kind of distortion on the background image, whereas in the original, the castle in the background always looked detailed. Maybe if you could recreate a completely identical scene with an identical (not just similar) castle and scenery, I’d believe that this is it, but right now I can't say that.

​Sorry, it's hard for me to express what exactly is wrong. It's like an uncanny valley feeling, e.g. everything seems to match the intention, yet somewhere deep down it feels like something is off and you can't explain what. One idea I have is to tell Claude to dig deeper into how visuals were rendered in Doom 1993 as pseudo-3D. It seems to me that the whole essence of such an identical rendering lies in the fact that it was an effect from Doom, just multiplied by better detail, creating that magic of immersion and the "diving" through the character's slow movement and smooth visual transition.

replies.author: yaosio
replies.body: I should have explained it better. The original idea was to go after that video, but then this came out of it and I really like what this looks like because it reminds me of 90s PC games  and so I went with it. I'm sorry! I should have been more clear about what I meant.

replies.author: Ravesoull
replies.body: Oh, ok. Then no questions. It's kinda classic, one replication idea  have produced another creative path in the process of the implementation. And that's good. Maybe someone found your shade really useful for their games. 🙂
